nameStory: The red maple earns its name from the spectacular crimson show it puts on in fall, often being the first tree to turn blazing red in New England's autumn display. But the 'red' doesn't stop there – its flowers, leaf stems, twigs, and even its seeds often carry shades of red throughout the year, making it truly red in every season.
description: Red maple is one of New England's most common and adaptable trees, growing 40-60 feet tall with a rounded crown. It's a medium-sized deciduous tree that can thrive almost anywhere – from swamps to dry ridges. The tree is famous for its brilliant fall colors and its ability to grow faster than most other maples, making it a pioneer species in disturbed areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-lobed leaves (sometimes 5-lobed) with sharp, pointed teeth along the edges. The leaf stems (petioles) are often bright red, and the leaves feel smooth and thin compared to sugar maple's thicker leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny red or yellow flowers appear in dense clusters before the leaves emerge in early spring. Male and female flowers usually grow on separate trees, creating clouds of color against bare branches.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Paired winged seeds (samaras) ripen in late spring to early summer, often with red wings. They're smaller than sugar maple seeds and drop earlier in the season, spinning like helicopters as they fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young bark is smooth and light gray, becoming darker and developing shallow furrows with age. The bark feels relatively thin and never gets as deeply ridged as sugar maple bark.

idTips.label: Twigs
idTips.description: Young twigs are often reddish and feel smooth to the touch. Buds are small, rounded, and typically red, arranged opposite each other on the branch.

habitat: Red maple is incredibly adaptable, growing in wet swamps, dry upland forests, and everything in between throughout New England. You'll find it from sea level to mountain slopes, often mixed with oak, pine, and birch. It thrives in acidic soils and can tolerate both flooding and drought better than most trees.

seasonality.spring: Small red or yellow flower clusters bloom before leaves emerge, creating colorful clouds in the canopy. New leaves unfold with reddish stems, and winged seeds develop quickly.
seasonality.summer: Seeds mature and drop by early summer, much earlier than other maples. Leaves are green with red stems, and the tree provides dense shade with its full crown.
seasonality.fall: Often the first tree to turn color, displaying brilliant reds, oranges, and yellows. Fall color can vary dramatically even between trees in the same area.
seasonality.winter: Identified by smooth gray bark, small red buds arranged opposite each other, and reddish twigs. Young trees often retain some dried leaves through winter.

funFact: Red maple trees can completely change their sex from year to year – a tree that produces only male flowers one year might produce female flowers the next, and some trees produce both male and female flowers simultaneously, making them nature's ultimate gender-fluid species.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with sugar maple, but red maple has sharper-toothed leaf edges and red leaf stems, while sugar maple has smooth leaf edges and green stems. Memory trick: 'Red maple = red stems and rough edges (teeth), Sugar maple = smooth edges and sweet sap.'
contextualKnowledge: Red maple is sometimes called 'soft maple' by woodworkers because its wood is less dense than sugar maple's 'hard maple.' Despite being in the soapberry family, red maples produce much less syrup-quality sap than sugar maples, though it can still be tapped.
compareHints: Red maple differs from sugar maple by its toothed leaf margins, red leaf stems, and earlier seed drop. Unlike silver maple, red maple's leaves aren't deeply cut or silvery underneath. Compared to Norway maple (non-native), red maple's leaf stems don't bleed milky sap when broken, and its seeds drop much earlier in the season.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its maple relatives, striped maple has the distinctive white-striped bark that no other North American maple possesses.
Among New England's maples, sugar maples have the smoothest leaf edges (no teeth) and the most rounded lobe shapes, while red maples have serrated edges and more pointed lobes.
Norway maple differs from sugar maple by its milky leaf sap, earlier and more chartreuse spring flowers, and wider-angled seed wings.
Box elder stands out dramatically from other New England maples because it's the only one with compound leaves instead of the classic lobed maple leaf shape.
Among New England's maples, mountain maple is the odd one out—it's the only one that stays truly shrubby and forms colonies rather than growing into a single-trunked tree.

Among New England maples, silver maple stands out for its deeply dissected leaves and silvery undersides - much more dramatic than the shallow lobes of red maple or the more rounded lobes of sugar maple.
Among New England maples, sycamore maple stands out for its exceptionally large leaves on long stalks and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England maples, Amur maple is unique for its consistently small size and three-lobed leaves with the distinctly elongated center lobe.

Japanese maple differs from all native New England maples by having much more deeply divided, delicate leaves with 5-9 narrow lobes compared to the broader, less-divided leaves of sugar maple, red maple, and silver maple.
Field maple is much smaller than sugar maple, red maple, or Norway maple, with distinctively small, thick, round-lobed leaves that set it apart from all other maples in New England.
